job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Capitol Policy Review. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Capitol Policy Review (CPR) is a nonpartisan, nonprofit newsroom based in Washington, DC, covering science and technology legislation in Congress. We publish explainers, vote trackers, and a weekly newsletter read by policy professionals. We do not take positions on legislation; our goal is accurate, fair, and useful coverage.

Current focus: One of our biggest stories this fall is S. 2817, the Superintelligence Prohibition Act. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
For our explainer ahead of next Thursday's markup, we want to cover the bill's weak spots. Can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Superintelligence Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Superintelligence Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COVERED AI SYSTEM.—The term "covered AI system" means—
  (A) an artificial intelligence model trained using a quantity of computing power greater than 10^26 integer or floating-point operations in a single training run; or
  (B) any artificial intelligence system that the Secretary determines is capable of substantially exceeding human performance across most cognitive tasks.
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED FACILITY.—The term "covered facility" means a data center containing more than 50,000 advanced AI chips.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to train, develop, or deploy a covered AI system.
(b) EXISTING SYSTEMS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to a covered AI system whose training began before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) SAFETY EVALUATION.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of safety evaluation.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered facility shall register the facility with the Department of Commerce.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the Department of Commerce a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the computing workloads run at the facility.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that covered AI systems can be developed safely.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
Based on the supplied text, the following are potential loopholes, ambiguities, and enforcement or litigation risks—not conclusions that a court would invalidate the bill. Existing federal law may supply some procedures and remedies, so omissions do not always mean enforcement is impossible.

### Coverage and definitions

1. **§ 2(1)(B)—Undefined decision-maker.** “The Secretary” is never defined. The references to Commerce in § 4 and the Secretary of State in § 6 leave uncertainty about who may designate systems as covered.

2. **§ 2(1)—Undefined core terms.** “Artificial intelligence,” “model,” and “system” are undefined, and the two coverage tests use different units: a model in paragraph (A), but a system in paragraph (B). It is unclear whether coverage attaches to individual components, an integrated product, or both.

3. **§ 2(1)(A)—Single-run limitation.** The compute test counts only a “single training run,” without defining that term or aggregating related runs. Multi-stage training, combinations of separately trained models, and other distributed development processes could fall outside this test, although the capability-based test might still apply.

4. **§ 2(1)(A)—Compute accounting is unspecified.** The bill calls an operation count a quantity of “computing power” and supplies no measurement method. It does not explain how to count different numerical precisions, sparsity, unsuccessful training work, or operations distributed across hardware and organizations.

5. **§ 2(1)(A)—Unclear treatment of post-training work.** The text does not say whether fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, distillation, or continuous learning counts as training or a separate run. That uncertainty affects both the compute threshold and the identity of the covered model.

6. **§ 2(1)(A)—Fixed threshold and strict cutoff.** Exactly \(10^{26}\) operations does not satisfy “greater than,” and there is no mechanism for updating the threshold. Improvements in computational efficiency could place increasingly capable models below it, leaving coverage dependent on a designation under paragraph (B).

7. **§ 2(1)(A)—Non-training compute is not expressly counted.** Substantial capabilities could come from inference-time computation, external tools, or orchestration rather than a qualifying training run. Such systems would depend on paragraph (B) for coverage.

8. **§ 2(1)(B)—Indeterminate capability standard.** “Substantially exceeding human performance across most cognitive tasks” specifies neither the human comparison group nor the universe, weighting, or measurement of tasks. It also leaves unclear whether capability is assessed with tools, scaffolding, or resource constraints.

9. **§ 2(1)(B)—Narrow but powerful systems may remain outside coverage.** A system that greatly exceeds humans in particular consequential domains would not necessarily exceed them across “most” cognitive tasks. Unless it meets the compute test, it may remain lawful under this bill.

10. **§ 2(1)(B)—Coverage depends on an affirmative determination.** Unlike paragraph (A), paragraph (B) requires the Secretary to determine capability. The bill sets no deadline or mandatory review process, potentially leaving qualifying systems outside that branch of coverage while action is delayed.

11. **§ 2(1)(B)—No designation procedure or scope rules.** The text does not specify notice, supporting evidence, when a designation takes effect, or whether it covers versions, derivatives, or a whole model family. Ordinary administrative-law review may apply, but the omissions create uncertainty and grounds for disputes.

12. **§§ 2(1), 3(a)—Unclear point at which training becomes prohibited.** Paragraph (A) describes a model “trained using” more than the threshold, while § 3 prohibits training it. The text does not clearly establish when work on a not-yet-covered model becomes unlawful or authorize a pre-training approval process.

### Persons and prohibited conduct

13. **§ 2(2)—Incomplete coverage of U.S.-connected persons abroad.** The definition includes citizens and state-organized corporations but not expressly permanent residents, noncitizen nationals, LLCs, partnerships, trusts, or federally organized entities. Those excluded categories remain covered when acting in the United States, but their activity abroad may not be.

14. **§§ 2(2), 3(a)—Foreign subsidiaries are not automatically covered abroad.** A foreign-incorporated subsidiary is not a “U.S. person” merely because a U.S. company owns it. A U.S. parent's own prohibited conduct could still create liability, but ownership or control alone is not expressly addressed.

15. **§ 3(a)—Unclear location rule for cross-border activity.** “Any person in the United States” does not establish where remote training, cloud-based development, or deployment occurs. Disputes could arise when personnel, corporate entities, servers, and users are in different countries.

16. **§ 3(a)—Undefined prohibited verbs.** “Train,” “develop,” and “deploy” are undefined. Their boundaries could determine whether research, testing, releasing model weights, providing API access, or modifying an existing system is prohibited.

17. **§ 3(a)—No express prohibition on possession or ordinary use.** The bill does not separately prohibit acquiring, possessing, accessing, or using a covered system. Whether customers using an existing or foreign service are “deploying” it is unresolved.

18. **§ 3(a)—Unclear responsibility for supporting activities.** Financing, supplying chips, hosting workloads, and providing technical assistance are not expressly prohibited as such. Existing criminal aiding-and-abetting or conspiracy rules may reach some knowing participation, but the bill does not define a corresponding civil rule or the duties of service providers.

### Exceptions

19. **§ 3(b)—Grandfathering exempts the entire system, not just existing work.** The exception says subsection (a) does not apply to a system whose training began before enactment. On its face, that permits subsequent training, development, and deployment of qualifying grandfathered systems without a stated endpoint.

20. **§ 3(b)—No meaningful-start requirement.** “Training began” has no minimum compute, expenditure, duration, or substantive-progress requirement. A limited pre-enactment start could support a claim to exemption for extensive later work.

21. **§ 3(b)—No boundary between an existing system and a new one.** The bill does not say whether major retraining, new versions, derivatives, or combinations of systems retain grandfathered status. That creates a potentially broad dispute over the continuing identity of an exempt system.

22. **§ 3(b)—No grandfathering documentation requirement.** The text requires no contemporaneous records, registration, or certification of a claimed pre-enactment start. Establishing eligibility could therefore depend on contested company records rather than a defined verification process.

23. **§ 3(c)—Safety evaluation is undefined.** There are no criteria distinguishing genuine safety evaluation from ordinary capability development or commercial testing. Activities serving both purposes could generate expansive exemption claims.

24. **§ 3(c)—The safety exception has no substantive limits.** It is not confined to particular evaluators, controlled settings, durations, or noncommercial activities. Because it exempts activities from all of subsection (a), it could encompass training, development, or deployment when conducted for the stated purpose.

25. **§ 3(c)—No approval or oversight mechanism.** Safety evaluators need not obtain authorization, report their activities, keep specified records, or satisfy containment requirements. The bill also does not allocate the burden of establishing the exception, leaving its administration to later interpretation.

### Facility registry

26. **§ 2(3)—Undefined chip category.** “Advanced AI chips” has no technical specification or update mechanism. Operators and enforcers could disagree over which processors, accelerators, or custom hardware count.

27. **§ 2(3)—Facility size is an imperfect coverage trigger.** The registry excludes facilities with exactly 50,000 qualifying chips or fewer, regardless of their aggregate compute capacity. A covered training workload could operate across multiple smaller facilities without any individually meeting the registration threshold.

28. **§§ 2(3), 4(a)—Unclear facility and operator boundaries.** The text does not define whether a campus, building, or separately managed installation is the relevant “data center.” Nor does it allocate registration duties among owners, tenants, cloud providers, and managers.

29. **§ 4(a)—Unspecified geographic scope.** Unlike § 3, the registry provision has no express territorial or nationality rule. Its application to overseas facilities, including those operated by U.S. companies, is uncertain.

30. **§ 4—No registration deadline or reporting specifications.** The bill does not say when initial registration is due, when quarterly reports must be filed, or how detailed a workload description must be. It does not expressly require customer identities, model identifiers, compute totals, or claimed exceptions.

31. **§ 4(b)—Reporting applies only to “registered” operators.** An operator that never registers would violate subsection (a), but could argue that subsection (b)'s separate reporting obligation never attached. “Each operator required to register” would avoid that textual gap.

32. **§§ 4, 5—Registry violations lack an express penalty.** Both penalty provisions apply only to violations of § 3. Failure to register or report therefore carries no penalty specified in this Act, although other law might address particular conduct, such as knowingly false submissions.

33. **§ 4—No express verification powers.** The bill supplies no inspection, audit, compulsory record-retention, or subpoena authority to verify workload reports or investigate unregistered facilities. Any such powers would have to come from another applicable source.

### Enforcement and legal challenges

34. **§§ 3–5—Enforcement responsibility and process are incomplete.** Commerce receives registrations, but the bill does not expressly identify who investigates prohibition violations or how civil penalties are assessed and collected. Existing federal authority may fill parts of that gap, but the Act leaves the enforcement framework underdeveloped.

35. **§ 5(a)—Civil culpability and violation counting are unclear.** Unlike the criminal provision, the civil provision states no mental-state requirement. “For each day” also leaves uncertain whether the maximum applies separately to each model, activity, or violation, complicating both compliance and penalty calculation.

36. **§ 5(a)—Monetary penalties may not ensure cessation.** The provision establishes a maximum, not a mandatory fine, and does not expressly provide profit disgorgement or a penalty tied to company size or economic benefit. For sufficiently valuable activity, the available monetary sanction may provide inadequate deterrence.

37. **§§ 3–5—No express shutdown or model-disposition remedy.** The Act does not expressly authorize emergency stop orders, injunctions, or disposition of unlawfully trained models and weights. Other authority may support some relief, but the bill does not itself explain how ongoing activity is stopped.

38. **§ 5(b)—Willfulness may be difficult to prove.** Criminal liability requires a willful violation, but the bill does not define that standard. Uncertain coverage, disputed designation notice, and broadly worded exceptions could make the required proof harder.

39. **§§ 2(1)(B), 3, 5(b)—Fair-notice and delegation challenges.** An open-ended agency capability determination would define conduct punishable by up to 10 years in prison, without clear measurement or designation rules. That combination invites vagueness, fair-notice, and potentially delegation challenges, though it does not establish that any would succeed.

40. **§§ 2(1)(A), 3(a)—Compute coverage is not tied to dangerous capability.** The compute branch can prohibit a model without any finding that it exceeds human performance or creates a safety risk. Depending on the regulated activity, that breadth could support statutory or constitutional challenges, including First Amendment arguments involving research or publication; those outcomes would be fact-dependent.

### Timing, international agreement, and duration

41. **§§ 5(a), 8—Conflicting start dates for civil liability.** Section 5(a) specifies violations occurring on or after enactment, while § 8 delays the Act's effectiveness by 180 days. The conflict creates uncertainty about conduct during that interval and whether Congress intended retroactive civil exposure.

42. **§§ 3(b), 8—The transition period treats systems differently.** Grandfathering turns on enactment, not the effective date. Systems whose training starts during the 180-day interval would lack the exception once the prohibition takes effect, with no express wind-down rule.

43. **§ 6—Negotiation does not guarantee foreign restrictions.** The Secretary of State must “seek to negotiate” an agreement, not secure one, and the 18-month language does not clearly specify whether negotiations must begin or conclude by then. There is no fallback if talks fail, while independent foreign activity outside U.S. jurisdiction remains beyond § 3.

44. **§ 6—No international verification or implementation framework.** “Equivalent” prohibitions are undefined, and the bill specifies no monitoring, enforcement, or domestic implementation mechanism for an agreement. An agreement would not, by this language alone, close foreign enforcement gaps.

45. **§ 7(a)—No process for obtaining the Academies report.** The bill neither commissions nor funds the report, sets a delivery deadline, nor defines what “developed safely” means. The stated early-termination mechanism therefore depends on an assessment the Act does not ensure will occur.

46. **§ 7(a)—Unclear consequences of early termination.** This subsection ends “the prohibition in section 3,” but does not expressly terminate the registry or explain treatment of pre-termination violations. It also leaves unclear whether “acting on” the report requires Congress to adopt its conclusions.

47. **§ 7(b)—Unconditional sunset overrides safety-based continuation.** The entire Act expires after 10 years even if Congress has made no safety finding. That ends prospective restrictions and registry obligations regardless of whether the bill's stated safety condition has been met.

48. **§ 7(b)—No tailored transition for outstanding matters.** The Act does not specify how pending enforcement, reporting obligations, or existing designations are handled at sunset. Federal saving-law principles may preserve accrued liabilities, so expiration should not be described as automatically erasing past violations.
